extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, regulators, and regulatory reform practitioners (Japan and comparative US observers)
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative analysis of regulatory process practices in Japan versus the United States, with emphasis on public comment, regulatory impact analysis, review of existing regulations, and central government coordination. Intended to identify 'good regulatory practices' and reforms to improve regulatory quality and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public consultation and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comment and transparency are consensus 'good regulatory practices' that contribute to trade, investment, and growth; public comment has been a critical feature of the U.S. system and is now required by law in Japan (since 2006) for proposed regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministries should publish proposed regulations for public comment to improve regulations by providing new information and ideas, and to increase transparency and accountability. Historically Japan lacked transparency and unwritten administrative guidance; reforms have reduced this and now require an opportunity for public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and timing of public comment periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Japan legally requires a 30-day comment period 'when possible', but ministries sometimes provide less time; the U.S. Presidential Executive Order recommends 60 days though practice varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment periods that are too short make it difficult to provide useful comments for complicated regulations. Sufficient notice (longer comment periods) is implied necessary for substantive input; short or rushed periods are an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine consideration of public comments (responsiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should be treated as a source of ideas and information to improve specific provisions of regulations, not merely as a formality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuing final regulations within a few days of the end of a comment period suggests comments were ignored (anti-pattern). Advisory councils (shingikai) and informal consultations can provide input but may function as rubber stamps; meaningful responsiveness requires mechanisms that show how comments affected outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) — core components
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical RIA components include a statement of the need for the regulation, an evaluation (and when possible, quantification) of the costs and benefits, and a comparison with alternative approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex-ante evaluation of regulations improves regulatory quality, deepens public understanding, and increases government accountability. Japan's guidance (2007) emphasizes these components and the importance of ex-ante analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and legal applicability of RIAs
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2007, RIAs have been required for parliamentary laws (horitsu) and Cabinet Orders (seirei), but not in practice for lower forms of regulation such as ministerial ordinances (shorei).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations in scope mean many impactful regulatory instruments may escape formal RIA requirements; extending RIA coverage is implied as a means to improve overall regulatory quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and timing of RIA implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: RIAs are often done to justify decisions already made rather than to inform draft regulations; many RIAs lack thorough economic analysis or serious evaluation of alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice is to conduct RIAs early (ex-ante) and use them to shape draft regulations. Submitting RIAs to a reviewing body before public issuance (rather than simultaneously) allows meaningful feedback. Doing RIAs post-hoc or superficially is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional incentives, authority, and review mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: No strong entity in Japan compels ministries to produce high-quality RIAs or to change draft regulations; MIC provides guidance and monitors compliance but has limited power to demand changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with U.S. OIRA, which reviews significant rules, shares drafts with other agencies and White House offices, and sets government-wide regulatory policies. Strong central coordination and authority (e.g., ability to review drafts, demand changes, and oversee policy) are recommended to improve consistency and quality. Proposed solutions include creating or empowering a Cabinet Office or expanding MIC's mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of existing regulations (regulatory review / deregulatory review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular, government-wide review of existing regulations to identify burdens and propose reforms has been an ongoing effort in Japan since the 1990s and was recently reinvigorated under the Cabinet Office for Promotion of Regulatory Reform; similar U.S. efforts were launched by Executive Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice includes soliciting ideas from outside government (e.g., open website hotline), producing lists of potential reforms with timelines for implementation, and institutionalizing the review process so it becomes routine rather than episodic. The U.S. initiative produced measurable near-term savings; institutionalization is a key challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central government coordination and cross-agency consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective coordination involves a central office that reviews important regulations, ensures consistency with executive priorities, shares drafts across agencies, and oversees government-wide regulatory policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Japan lacks a direct analogue to OIRA's specific role; enhancing coordination mechanisms (e.g., draft-sharing, interagency comment, executive-level prioritization) helps ensure benefits justify costs and promotes coherent regulatory policy across ministries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucratic capacity, expertise, and staffing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministries may lack staff with the necessary expertise or training to conduct thorough RIAs, and frequent rotation of bureaucrats (every ~two years) makes it difficult to develop relevant expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Building capacity through training, longer staff tenure in regulatory roles, and retaining expertise are implied prerequisites for producing high-quality, consistent RIAs and for meaningful use of public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce unwritten administrative guidance and publish proposed regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, Japanese regulation relied on unwritten administrative guidance; reforms have sought to reduce such practices and require publication of proposed regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing proposals increases transparency and public access. Continuing efforts to replace informal, unwritten guidance with formal, published proposals is a quality-improving practice.
